content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) initiated the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) in the 1970s in collaboration with the cruise ship industry. This program was designed to assist the cruise industry in developing and implementing comprehensive sanitation protocols aimed at reducing the risk of acute gastroenteritis outbreaks. Vessels with foreign itineraries carrying 13 or more passengers are subject to biannual inspections and, if necessary, re-inspections. From the early 1970s to 1986, the program included inspections at U.S. ports. However, portions of the program were discontinued by the CDC in 1986. Due to pressure from the cruise industry and the public, Congress directed the CDC to reinstate the program. Responsibility for the VSP was transferred to the CDC’s National Center for Environmental Health (NCEH) in 1986. Public meetings were held to gather input from the public and the cruise industry, leading to the launch of a restructured program on March 1, 1987. The program became self-funded, with inspection fees based on vessel size. In 1989, the VSP published an Operations Manual to guide the cruise industry in educating shipboard personnel. This manual was based on the FDA’s 1976 model food service code and the World Health Organization’s Guide to Ship Sanitation. By 1998, updates to the manual were deemed necessary due to advancements in food safety science, changes in the FDA Food Code, and new technologies in the cruise industry. Over the next two years, the VSP sought input from the cruise industry, public health experts, and the FDA to ensure the revised 2000 manual addressed current public health concerns. A similar process was undertaken to update the manual in 2005. Despite the 2005 manual being in use for nearly six years, emerging pathogens, new technologies, and advancements in food science necessitated further revisions. The 2011 VSP Operations Manual incorporated feedback from government and private industry partners, as well as the public. The CDC expressed gratitude to all contributors and emphasized its commitment to keeping the manual current through ongoing public review and updates as new information and technologies emerge. The VSP fosters collaboration between the cruise industry and government to identify and mitigate health risks associated with vessels, ensuring a clean and safe environment for passengers and crew. The cruise industry’s proactive efforts to maintain high standards of food safety and sanitation are critical to protecting public health. The program conducts continuous surveillance of acute gastroenteritis (AGE) cases and coordinates outbreak investigations on vessels. It also provides food safety and sanitation training for ship and shore personnel, consults on renovation and construction plans, and disseminates public health information. The VSP Operations Manual serves as the foundation for program operations and inspections, with periodic reviews to address emerging public health issues and technological advancements. The manual requires vessels to maintain records on medical incidents, potable and recreational water, food safety, and housekeeping for 30 days to one year. These records are reviewed during inspections. Violations, such as producing water in polluted areas, can result in point deductions during inspections. Definitions and guidelines in the manual clarify terminology and provide detailed standards for food safety, water quality, and sanitation practices. The manual also includes specific definitions for terms such as acute gastroenteritis, which refers to sudden-onset symptoms like diarrhea, vomiting, fever, abdominal cramps, headache, or muscle aches. An AGE outbreak is defined as cases exceeding 3% of passengers or crew or involving two or more laboratory-confirmed cases linked to food or water consumption during a cruise. Isolation of symptomatic crew members is mandatory, while isolation of symptomatic passengers is advised to prevent the spread of illness. The manual outlines standards for food preparation, storage, and service areas, as well as water systems, pest management, and waste disposal. It emphasizes the importance of maintaining sanitary conditions to minimize health risks. The VSP continues to adapt its guidelines to reflect advancements in science, technology, and public health practices, ensuring the safety and well-being of all individuals on board cruise vessels.
